utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And now the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber bids welcome to all those present, representatives of the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, the registrar, and all those in the courtroom, without forgetting those outside, that is, the interpreters and the technicians. We need to continue today the hearing of yesterday's witness, and I'm going to ask Madam Usher to be kind enough to bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today's hearing will be devoted to the continuation of the cross-examination, and I will give the floor to the Defence counsel, who has questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Major Kent-Payne.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We broke off yesterday with questions regarding the general situation in Central Bosnia at the time of your arrival and some other general matters of significance for the defence of General Hadzihasanovic. I should now like to go back to your testimony during the examination-in-chief. In answer to a question from the President of the Trial Chamber and my learned friends, you said that you drew your conclusions on the basis of intelligence information gathered by your intelligence officers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The source of information for you were your observations while patrolling the region; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. From my own observations and that of all the other vehicle commanders tasked with gathering information from our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The source of your knowledge was also the conversations you had with civilian and other authorities in the area of responsibility of your battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: One of your sources were also data that you exchanged with other international organisations and European monitors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not qualified to comment on that. That would have taken place between the intelligence -- or the military information officer and the agencies that you've mentioned. I was not personally involved with that, so cannot comment on how often this took place or whether indeed it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also got some information from your interpreters and the local staff employed by your battalion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't comment on whether that would be the case. As far as information coming from the -- from the interpreters, they were strictly briefed that they should not act as intelligence-gatherers themselves but merely act as a mouthpiece for the commander to which they were working.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, all the information that you and your colleagues gathered during the day were summarised in the military reports, daily reports; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, you had meetings every evening in the battalion, usually held by Lieutenant Colonel Duncan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. These meetings would happen at 6.00 each evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the meetings, all of you would present your daily observations.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the milinfosum, your observations were contained, as well as comments by the person tasked to analyse that information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These milinfosums also included information that Lieutenant Colonel Duncan gathered from meetings with representatives of the army and the Croatian Defence Council; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this information contained in the milinfosums were a part of your overall information on which you based your conclusions; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you did not have the authority, nor the means and resources, to verify what other colleagues were saying, nor what was contained in the milinfosums; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm sorry, I don't understand the -- the question. Yes, there would be no means to verify this, but there would also be no -- there would be no way of thinking that's -- the information that was given by military colleagues would not be correct to the best of their knowledge. They certainly wouldn't make up details. Those details would have been reported to them, and they took that in the best of faith.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I'm not at all implying that any one of you would pass on information differently from what it was originally. But your sources could have been reliable or not reliable; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But if a -- if a single piece of information was given that we had not heard before, then the military information staff would target patrols to verify that particular information. It's most unlikely that any actions would have been taken on a single piece of information. That's not the way the military works there, and we would seek to verify any single piece of information before taking action upon that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In your area, in all the municipalities there were civilian authorities and the civilian police; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At times you communicated with them as well, but you didn't devote any particular attention to the competencies that those bodies had on the ground. Would it be right to say that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, that is correct, but each individual piece of information would be verified before any action was taken on that. Clearly some of the sources were much more reliable than others. One side would say something against the other side, which quite often would be completely untrue, which was why every statement was -- was verified to the best of our ability before we either believed it or most certainly took action on those statements. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, during your term of office, being military men, you most often addressed military authorities, regardless of whether a particular issue was within their terms of reference or not.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not the case either, because we would -- we generally found that the military would not often give the correct situation. They would give the situation that they wanted us to believe, and we would take every step to verify what they'd said, usually by talking to the village elders, be they the priest or the Imam or simply the older people in the village, who in many cases could be more -- could be more relied upon to give us the correct picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us now move on to the 15th of May, about which you spoke in detail. You said that on the 15th of May you decided to go with your company to areas in which you had assumed representatives of the UNPROFOR had still not visited; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, again, that's -- that's not entirely correct. I wish to once more emphasise, as I did in my earlier testimony, that it was not a question of me deciding, that these tasks were given to us by the battalion operations officer and the battalion information officer, then. It was they who decided where the patrols should go to, because as I said earlier, they had the honesty traces of the Cheshire Regiment's patrols and therefore they decided where we should go based on the information that there were -- that they had and that they could identify the areas where there had been no patrols in the last few months.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for those points of clarification. I'm obviously too much of a civilian, so I often forget that a soldier always acts upon orders and assignments. But you have now explained that. Thank you. At that point in time, you had been in Bosnia and Herzegovina for a month already, that is, in the area of Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When going on assignment, in spite of all the above-listed sources of information, you had no knowledge about the presence of Mujahedin in the area, had you?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, you managed to visit Travnik and the surrounding locations close to the main road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. During our period of familiarisation, we had travelled extensively around our area, though in most cases this was the main centres of population, so that we would be familiar with both the routes through our areas to make it easier for us to escort convoys, and also the locations of the various local headquarters. So if we had to pick up a local commander, we would know where his headquarters was and also know where he was if we needed to go and talk to him about something.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After your arrival in Zenica, brigade commander -- a brigade commander was kidnapped, the commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade, and it was known that this kidnapping had been done by the Mujahedin. You were aware of that, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I've heard of this. If I was told about it, I certainly don't remember it at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Mujahedin could occasionally be seen on the streets of Travnik. Did you see them in those days?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO frequently spoke about the Mujahedin and addressed protests to UNPROFOR. Were you aware of those protests?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, again, I was not aware of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of April, 1993, in your area, in the village of Miletici, a crime occurred and it was immediately known that it had been committed by the Mujahedin. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said in my earlier testament, the first indication that I personally had that there were Mujahedin in my area was when I met up with these people on the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that in spite of the fact that you had an elaborate system of information, you had received no information about the existence of the Mujahedin prior to your going on assignment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to your own testimony, you were first stopped by members of the regular Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Han Bila; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you, as you have a map in front of you, and for your movements to be clear to Their Honours, could you please indicate the place called Han Bila, where you were stopped for the first time.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spent half an hour there talking and persuading the commander to allow you to continue on your way; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe I said that it was much longer than that. We were there for at least one hour, in -- both talking to people outside at the checkpoint and then inside with the local commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I heard you correctly - and that can be found on page 25 of the LiveNote - you said that when you went out, you saw that about 30 or 40 soldiers had gathered and about a hundred civilians, who were in a friendly mood in relation to you. Is that what you stated yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was for you an event and a fact that you have remembered because it was important for you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was unusual to see so many people there, and also it appeared that for them also it was unusual to see -- see United Nations vehicles, because in that -- in that early part of the tour, we were clearly something of a curiosity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even though this stop there for almost one hour was unusual for you, nevertheless you didn't immediately inform your command about having encountered a certain problem; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would not have been the case, because in the second vehicle was the patrol second-in-command, and his task was to give constant updates back to the battle group headquarters as to our position. I obviously could not do that myself, being in the local commander's building and negotiating with him, but my -- the second-in-command of the patrol, as what we call a standard operating procedure, would update the battalion headquarters every few -- every few minutes with progress as to what was happening. This could be in the form of a positive report, and an example of that would be: We have now moved through the checkpoint and our location is at the following village; or a negative report, which would simply be we are still at the checkpoint and there is no progress at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After finally gaining permission to move on, you started off and 6 kilometres later you came across a checkpoint where there was one guard and a regularly positioned barrier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Although, there were two guards, in fact, because one stayed on the barrier and the second went off to fetch his local commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in answer to a question from the Prosecution, you said that the soldier at the checkpoint wouldn't let you pass and that he said that he had to ask his commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He told us that he could not get us -- he could not allow us through and the standard response to that from me or any other patrol commander would be, "In that case, please will you fetch your local commander so I can talk to him."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When that person arrived, whom you thought to be the local commander, you said that he informed you that you could pass through the checkpoint only with the approval of the 3rd Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said we needed a -- a piece of paper, written permission from the corps headquarters to move through to the north of that -- that particular checkpoint. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This answer is also something you remembered well because you believed that UN forces had the right to free movement and that you didn't need anybody's permission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. On our training, we'd been told that the act of going to get a piece of paper should not be done or should only be done as a last resort because this was -- this would give a sort of legitimacy to the perceived control over the United Nations that the local forces would have if they were to give permission for UN forces to go to any location.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you confirmed that on the 10th of May, 2000 you gave a statement to the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal. Is it true that these important facts that you noticed during your first patrol, about which you testified yesterday, that is, that when you left there were more than a hundred people gathered there and that you had to have a permit from the 3rd Corps to pass, these were facts that you didn't tell the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal on that occasion? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did not tell him because he didn't ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that these two or three guards at the checkpoint were shortly joined by some civilians; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Again, it would appear that we were a curiosity and a number of people who appeared to be civilians, including some women, appeared at the checkpoint to look at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In Han Bila nor at this checkpoint, you did not see any insignia of the soldiers who were present of the army or the brigade that they belonged to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Shortly a Toyota vehicle arrived, from which foreigners emerged.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They first chased away the civilians, and then they addressed the local men in uniform and issued them some sort of an order; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Although, the order was not a verbal order; it was more of a -- a series of gestures, indicating what the individual wished the militiamen to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These local soldiers obeyed these orders given by gestures, and it was quite obvious that they feared these foreigners; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That -- that would be my interpretation of the situation, that they were anxious to comply with the orders that were being given to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to your testimony, there may have been between 40 and 50 foreign soldiers there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ultimately, yes. Although, they did not appear all at once. They -- they filtered into the area over the time that I was negotiating with both the local -- with the -- the local commander initially and then the Arabic gentleman, who came out of the Toyota after a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the evening, at your regular meeting you reported about what had happened to you that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was your judgement that you were close to the village of Fazlici, several hundred metres away from that village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We were -- our intention was to turn -- turn down this small track here to the village of Suhi Dol, and we were stopped just short of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very close to the place where you were stopped is a locality called Poljanice; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- I can confirm that by looking at the map, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After this incident, you sought to find out who the foreigners in the area were; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct either. The military information staff sought to find out who the foreigners were, and they tasked their own agencies to find out who these people were. They also tasked us, as in the -- the patrols out on the ground, to ask questions about these people. And the battalion ops officer also issued an instruction that there were to be no more patrols into that area due to the obvious risk from these particularly aggressive people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your subsequent information led you to find out that in -- close to Mehurici, in a location called Poljanice, was a camp of foreign soldiers, that is, the Mujahedin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As more information emerged, we received more regular briefings on these people, and we were told by the military information officer that their role in this location was to train regular BiH soldiers and that it was the -- the training camp that we had blundered into inadvertently in the area north of Han Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, the real information that you received at the time indicated that a part of the local Muslim population was joining the Mujahedin and that the Mujahedin were training them, especially younger men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not as I recall that, but I -- I would not confirm or deny that, as I cannot -- I cannot remember those exact details. All I remember is that we were told that it was a training camp and that the Mujahedin were training soldiers there. Whether they were in fact local population or not, we would have probably taken the view that if you train the local population, then they, too, become soldiers. But I'm afraid I do not recall the exact -- the exact details of this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of military information, you certainly knew that in the area a brigade of the BH army was active; that is, the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid I do not recall the exact number of the brigade, but -- but yes, it would have been clear to us that there was a BiH brigade in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This incident and event was something you did not try and inform the brigade commander about, the commander of that particular brigade.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, personally that would not be my duty to do that. The way that the battalion operated was that each location had a liaison officer and that it was the liaison officer's task to liaise with the local brigade commander. The company commanders, of whom I was -- I was one, were in charge of the patrols and the convoy escorts, and it would not generally have been our task to report such information to the brigade commanders. The chain of command that we employed was for the patrol commanders to report to the military information officer, who would report to the operations officer and the commanding officer, who would task a liaison officer to visit the relevant -- the relevant brigade headquarters. And I'm afraid I can't confirm whether that happened in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in answer to one of my questions, you said that when you arrived in Vitez the HVO had already suppressed most of the Bosnian population out of the Lasva River Valley; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From places of Vitez with the exception of Stari Vitez, Busovaca, Kaonik, and other towns that were immediately close to the Lasva River.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In fact, the majority of this movement had taken place in the -- in the Busovaca Valley. However, there was still at this stage some cooperation between the HVO and the -- and the BiH. And one example of that would be the checkpoint at Dolac, which is here -- there, and also the checkpoint at the -- the garage in Travnik, the petrol station, which at the early stage of our tour were still joint checkpoints with BiH and HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you can certainly confirm that after the massacre in Ahmici the BH army could not pass along the main road via Vitez and Busovaca towards the Lasva overpass; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, as members of the UNPROFOR, you started receiving information that the HVO was starting to cooperate with Serb forces against the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm whether I was told that or not. My recollection of this period is that in the very early stages of our tour part of the front line with the Serb forces in the area of Turbe was held jointly by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. HVO and BiH troops. But due to the tension following the Ahmici massacre, the BiH -- wrong, the HVO troops withdrew from this cooperation, then. If there were reports of cooperation between the HVO and the Serbs, I'm afraid I do not remember this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to abandoning the front at Turbe, the HVO also abandoned other front lines on Mount Vlasic, above the villages on the slopes running down to the Bila River; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, the HVO abandoned all their front line positions with the Serbs at around the -- the late May, early June period. So that would be correct. There would be, as I understand it, no HVO troops on the front line with the Serbs, and the front line with the Serbs was held solely by the BiH during this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this was a front line running along several hundred kilometres, this created additional problems for the BH army, which was anyway rather poorly armed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The -- as we were briefed, the problem that the BiH had was not lack of manpower but lack of weapons and equipment for that manpower. And we would often see soldiers going to the front line and taking over a rifle from another soldier and then they would go back to -- to a resting area without any weapons at all. So yes, there was clearly a problem for the BiH in manning such a long stretch of the front line once the HVO had ceased to cooperate in action against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of your tour of the area, you were also able to see that HVO units were starting to dig in around Croatian villages and especially on passes that linked Zenica with Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 3rd Corps sent to UNPROFOR almost on a daily basis protest reports because of this conduct by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I cannot comment on that, as those -- those protests would not have come directly to me. But I can imagine that he would do so, because he would want UNPROFOR to keep the roads open.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were also aware that at Ovnak an HVO checkpoint had been set up and that the line had been fortified from Ovnak via Grahovcici with trenches and dugouts placed there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that. And I saw some of these defensive positions myself when I visited that village. This was not unusual in the area, and the front line at this stage was being fortified by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were also able to note that on elevations that controlled the Bila Valley, such as Strmac, Usice, the HVO had positioned heavy weapons on those features; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't comment on that, because, as I mentioned earlier in my testimony, at this stage the HVO were extremely uncooperative, and in the majority of cases would not allow UNPROFOR patrols into areas which they considered to be sensitive. And as a particular example of that, I used the hill at Cifluk and the HVO front line along the -- the west -- sorry, the western side of the Bila Valley in the area of Pokrajcici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At your daily meetings, you were informed by the liaison officer of your battalion that as early as the beginning of May the HVO had moved its forces to heights above Travnik, that they had directed their heavy weapons towards the town and had virtually surrounded the town of Travnik. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were also informed that at checkpoints in Guca Gora and at Ovnak the HVO is turning back members of the army who were going to take up their shift on the front line, which resulted in the fact that soldiers could not be replaced, even after three weeks.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have no recollection of that detail, but it would not surprise me that that was an action taken by the HVO at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are certainly familiar with the information that is contained in your milinfosum of the 1st of June, number 33, that at the -- an HVO checkpoint the commander of the operative group Bosanska Krajina was stopped and harassed.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid I don't recall the individual details of this, but what I do remember is that around this time we were tasked with carrying a number of BiH commanders to various meetings because they could no longer move freely through checkpoints manned by the HVO. So while I don't remember the individual incident which you've just remembered, I do remember that we had to carry out a number of escort duties for the reasons which you describe.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To remind you of this event, I would kindly ask you to look at the milinfosum number 33, dated the 1st of June, 1993, in view of the fact that these are facts about which you were informed at your regular meetings. So could you look at this milinfosum which we received, Your Honours, by examining the archives of the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could this milinfosum be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please look at the report concerning Travnik municipality, the paragraph related to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm reading this at the moment. Yes, I've read the piece you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Major, that the arrest, disarming, and harassment of a commander of an operative group for any army, including the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was a very important incident?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would be a most serious incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, you certainly were aware that immediately after that, at the Ovnak checkpoint, eight buses with members of the BH army were stopped and turned back to Zenica, though they were going to replace soldiers who were on the front line at Turbe? Is that a fact you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm -- I was not aware of that fact. If I can explain perhaps for the benefit of the Presidents of the Court. The preceding item on this, the Maglaj incident, I was personally involved in that incident, both in the initial shelling of the United Nations convoy and in the operations to recover the bodies of the drivers. This operation lasted for approximately two days, which would possibly explain why I don't have any immediate recollection of the items which are referred to in the paragraph on Travnik. However, I have no doubt that as this is in our milinfosum, this is correct. But I'm saying this is the first that I've seen this in this detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, although the witness said that this is the first time that he sees this incident described in detail, he did nevertheless confirm that this is a milinfosum and that this is a serious incident that could have happened to a particular military. We would like to move to have it admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has no objection to this milinfosum being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Major, would you please put your name and today's date on this document that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, Major, if I tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Before you continue, we need to give this document an exhibit number. This document, drafted on the 1st of June, 1993, please let's have an exhibit number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, in view of the fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Excuse me for the interruption, Mr. President, but the transcript did not capture the exhibit number of the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit number is DH70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, since the army could not use the road by Bila, the only alternative route for communication between Travnik and Zenica was the one across Guca Gora and Ovnak; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And this was identified by our military information staff as being an important main supply route for the BiH linking Zenica and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the army, as you have already said while giving evidence, was squeezed in the area between the Lasva Valley and Mount Vlasic, the attacks of the HVO and the blockades they carried out on this road practically rendered it impossible for the army to remain in that area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And because of the interruptions to this main supply route there, as I recall, the military information staff and the commanding officer held meetings with both HVO and BiH commanders to ensure if possible that this route remained open. When the HVO were obstructive towards this, I believe that -- that the BiH were asked whether they were going to do something about this road, and this was the reason for the meetings between the commanders. As I said, I was not at that meeting, but the result of that, which we were briefed, was that there had been a cease-fire agreed and that this road would remain open.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As an officer, you certainly find it much clearer than we civilians can, the fact that when a military commander when faced with such problems has to engage in long-term planning in order to be able to respond to enemy attacks, those that make it impossible for him to control his own territory, to carry out defence tasks, and to defend his own people. Isn't that the way a commander would act under normal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is entirely correct. And we, as the more senior officers in the British Battalion, would try and put ourselves in the minds of the local commanders to try and guess what they were going to do next. And it was obvious that 3 Corps could not tolerate a situation where troops in Travnik were cut off from troops in Zenica with no supply route between the two, and it was obvious to us that if an agreement could not be reached between the two sides, that one side or the other would have to do something about this route.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can agree with me when I say that the orders of the military commanders of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were to seek a peaceful settlement but also that if there is an attack, they have to respond to the attack and defend this major communication route; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that would have been the case for any army in a similar situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are aware that on the 4th of June the HVO attacked the town of Travnik from the positions where the heavy artillery had been. Do you know that? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And we sent vehicles and patrols into that area to monitor this situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of June, the HVO attacked the village of Velika Bukovica as well, and from those positions they could also control the town of Travnik; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And I myself was in Travnik at this stage, being shelled by -- from positions that we believed to have been held by the HVO. And at the same time, our commanding officer and liaison officers were doing their best to broker a cease-fire to stop this shelling of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO attack against Velika Bukovica led to the imprisonment of a large number of civilians, and according to initial information there were 18 civilians killed but later it was established that it was 8 civilians who were killed. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall this fact. Although, if it is -- if it is confirmed as being true, I would not be surprised if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to previous plans of the defence that was being prepared in case there would be an attack, the army did respond to these attacks and the fighting spread to the entire area between Travnik and Zenica; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Although, that's not as I recall the -- the way that it happened. As I recall, the attack in the -- in the Bila Valley were a separate operation to that of -- of the area of Travnik there. But again, my -- my actual recollection of this is not that distinct because there was a lot of fighting going on, both in -- in Travnik and in the Bila Valley. And my understanding of this was that there were two -- two separate operations there, one going on in Travnik itself and one in the Bila Valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show on the map where Velika Bukovica is.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have absolutely no idea. I would hope someone could show me to jog my memory on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to take a look at the map, and you can see above Travnik, a bit lower in relation to Maljine, so between Travnik and Maljine, that's where the village is. So to the west of Guca Gora. That's where the village of Velika Bukovica is. And we discussed it earlier on. As you testified yourself, this was a place that the attack took place at on the 5th of June. Is it true that on the 7th of June the Muslim village of Bandol was attacked and burned down?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can go back to your earlier comment and just clarify this. I'm afraid that as British soldiers our intimate knowledge of Serbo-Croat was not great at this stage, and we would have referred to that village as Bukovica, which is the way in which it is written on the map. I've no doubt the actual name of the village is -- is Velika Bukovica, but it's not written on the map, so that's not how we referred to it. To move on to your second question, yes, I'm well aware of the attack on Bandol. I was at that village perhaps four or five days before the attack, and I asked the local militia whether they required any assistance, whether they needed any help from UNPROFOR, and was told that this was not the case. And after the evacuation of Guca Gora on the 8th of June, I was approached by -- by a local man -- by a local Muslim from a -- a village close by, the village of - again, excuse my pronunciation - Krpeljici, which is here, and told that there had been an attack on Bandol and that UNPROFOR should -- should visit this because there was a chance that it had been another situation similar to that in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of my previous question, you can certainly confirm that both Velika Bukovica and Bandol are villages that were in the broader area of the Bila and that this took place a day after the defence activities of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina continued on the 8th of June.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you answered my questions that had to do with your knowledge, in terms of what happened in the village of Bandol, and you did this at your own initiative, could you please look at the 13th of June milinfosum, which contains the information you provided about what you saw in the village of Bandol. Major, this is paragraph (e) that contains that particular information provided by you.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I recognise this information, because it would have been provided by -- by me myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please keep this milinfosum for a while, because I will have additional questions with regard to that particular document. Thank you. So you said that on the 8th of June you were not in Guca Gora but that there was another company of yours that was there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not as I recall my testimony. What I believe I said was that on the 7th of June the call signs from "A" Company were in Guca Gora, commanded by Lieutenant Medley. On the afternoon of the 7th of June I was tasked to take a convoy of lorries to Guca Gora but was advised to turn back because of the firing and the shooting that was going on in Guca Gora. I actually myself went to Guca Gora on the 8th of June, then, when I took my convoy of 16 armoured vehicles

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, since in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor you referred to the date of the 8th of June, when Company "A" received information, and to the 9th of June, when you came to take over these civilians from the monastery, is it possible that there was a mistake in the date that you specifically referred to yesterday before the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is entirely possible. As I recall - and I would need to check my diary, which I made at the time for the exact date of this, that what I do recall was that one day, either the 7th or the 8th of June, was when the incident took place with "A" Company and that my involvement in this was the day after.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you left Guca Gora with civilians and some of the members of the HVO and the clergyman, the monastery had not been damaged; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You took with you some important objects from the monastery. This is what the clergyman asked you to do, but you knew that most of the valuable objects from the monastery had been relocated to a safe location earlier on; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, no. All I recall was that the abbot in charge of the monastery asked our regimental padre to move whatever items he could from the church. And this is what we did by putting onto the lorry that was carrying the baggage of -- i.e., the suitcases of those people who were evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now let us go back to your testimony regarding the 13th of June of 1993, when you came to Guca Gora again. You said that the task of your mission was to get to Maljine because according to the information that you had received from several persons, at that particular locality the Mujahedin had committed a crime and that there was perhaps even a mass grave there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I do not know the exact source of this information. The briefing that I was given by the -- by the UN civilian representative, Randy Rhodes, and the liaison officer, Captain Mark Bower, was that someone had been handed a sketch map and Captain Bower showed me this sketch map and my task as the patrol commander was to take them to the village of Maljine, to search and either verify or dispute this allegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were accompanied by Randy Rhodes, an officer in charge of civilian affairs, and Captain Mark Bower; is that right? They accompanied you when you were carrying out this task.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also with you were some journalists and your interpreter; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And a number of armoured vehicles, which I recall as being six. So each vehicle would have contained five soldiers, so we would have had with us approximately 30 soldiers, Randy Rhodes and Mark Bower, one female interpreter, and as I recall, three members of the press.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you came to Guca Gora, you could notice that the Croat population had left the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Because I'd physically taken them out myself a few days earlier, and so it came as no surprise that there were no Croat civilians in this village any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You noticed that there had been thefts, that the abandoned houses had been looted.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not notice that. I was too busy negotiating with the -- with the foreign soldiers to have any time to go into any of the buildings. So if there was looting that had taken place, I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, it was quite clear - and that is what you reported at the meeting, and that is stated in your milinfosum too - that there had been no destruction of houses in Guca Gora at the moment when you arrived there.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you came to Guca Gora, as you said in your testimony, you noticed a group of armed persons, foreigners, in front of the monastery and around it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that's -- I don't believe that's what I said. My recollection is that there were a group of soldiers around the monastery who were clearly foreigners, but mingled amongst them were soldiers who by their appearance appeared to be both -- to both be Bosnians and also members of the local militia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your convoy had been stopped and a large number of these foreigners were around your vehicle; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They established that they had a machine-gun nest behind the sandbags and it was obvious that their attitude was hostile; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They refused to let you through; although, you explained the purpose of your mission to them in detail; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct also.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These foreigners were wearing a variety of clothing. Some of them had Arab headdress; others had trousers that reminded you of the Turkish or Afghan-type of trousers. So this was a mix of civilian and military uniforms. I mean, what these persons wore. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The people who were obviously foreigners were dressed like that. Other people present there were dressed as -- in the manner of normal BiH militiamen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the Mujahedin saw journalists, that made them particularly angry; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't believe that's what I said. When the Mujahedin saw the film cameraman, they became particularly agitated at the prospect of being filmed. I then told the film cameraman to get into the back of the vehicle and detailed one of my soldiers to ensure that he did not come out of the vehicle again. The two -- the two written press reporters - and by that, I mean newspaper reporters - continued to walk around at this stage, and there was no aggression shown towards them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These foreigners started insulting both you and the United Nations; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, if I can go back to how I recall my testimony of yesterday. One individual foreigner insulted the United Nations, which was the man who was clearly, in my opinion, from Yorkshire, and it was him who insulted us, not -- not foreigners, plural.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I obviously didn't understand you quite correctly yesterday. After a lengthy talk with these foreigners, you asked whether your vehicles were the problem or the fact that you were heading towards Maljine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. When the gentleman of Arab appearance appeared, this was the -- the details of the discussion that I had with him, and it was him who I asked whether, as you quite rightly say, it was the vehicles or simply myself and the other officers who he objected to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, before you asked him that, an incident occurred, that is, a bullet was fired accidentally by one of the soldiers present, and your marksman also pointed his weapon towards that group; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry to talk semantics about my statement of yesterday. What you say is correct, that one of the militiamen did fire his weapon. However, the term "marksman" is incorrect. I believe what I said yesterday was that the vehicles traversed their turrets, i.e., the part of the vehicle that hold it is armament - in this case, it would have been to the left - to point at the militiamen and the -- the foreigners, to -- to display a more aggressive posture in what we initially believed to be a shot fired against our people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm obviously not familiar with all the terms that you are using as a soldier. But this was the most critical moment during this conversation with the foreigners; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. If I can expand on this, perhaps for the benefit of the nonmilitary people here: I myself was outside my vehicle at the time, so I saw the incident and was immediately aware that this had been a single bullet fired accidentally into the ground. However, the soldiers in the other vehicles would have been inside the -- the turrets of their vehicles, almost certainly with the hatches closed down, and to them all they heard was a shot, and initially they would have no idea as to whether that was an accidental discharge or directed at them. So they responded in the manner of trained soldiers and traversed their turrets to counter the perceived threat. As trained soldiers as well, they did not immediately return fire but waited to assess the situation and also waited from orders from me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, the situation calmed down and you were allowed to start off in your Toyota, to carry out your assignment, while the vehicles stayed on in Guca Gora; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even though this situation that we have described was a very dangerous one, you nevertheless decided to move on armed with only a single pistol that was concealed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I myself only had a single pistol. Captain Bower also carried a pistol. Randy Rhodes, being a civilian, was unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you, Randy Rhodes, and Captain Bower set off in a Toyota truck and with this Arab person, virtually without any more significant weaponry.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I would also like to clarify. There were in fact three -- three foreigners in the front of the vehicle: The Arab gentleman, the person who spoke broken English that I'd initially spoken to, and the third person, who was driving the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were aware of the risk you were running and which your colleagues also were exposed to, that is, Randy Rhodes and Captain Bower, going in an unknown direction with unknown people, people unknown to you.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But the three of us decided that in this case the risk was worth taking in order to -- to fulfil our task.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How great the risk was is best illustrated by the fact that you gave clear instructions to your second-in-command what he should do if you should not return without [as interpreted] an hour or if anything should happen to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first time when you encountered foreigners on the 15th of May, you realised that they had a hostile attitude towards the United Nations and that they were not prepared to make any major concessions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On that day too, the same person was present that you had met on the 15th of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The decision that you took when you set off was not a customary one for a soldier because he exposed himself and his co-combatants and civilians to an uncertain fate and to danger; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is only half correct there. The reason why I took that decision was that the Arab gentleman was clearly in a more conciliatory mode. When the first time I met him, he refused to give any ground whatsoever. On this second occasion, he agreed to our request to let us -- to let us visit the village of Maljine. I took this to be a sign that he was willing to cooperate, and in the terms that we use in the military, pushed open a door that was slightly open. By that I mean I used the -- his cooperation to exploit that and go along with the task in order to attempt to complete it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached the village of Maljine, you noticed a group of civilians who were looting. And when they noticed you, they started running away. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall making that statement in my statement of yesterday. What I believe I said was that on the way to Maljine we passed groups of civilians and the Arab gentleman in the front of the vehicle shook his fist out of the window and shouted "Allah-U-Ekber," and the civilians responded in kind. If there was any looting going on in Maljine, I certainly didn't see this and I don't believe I mentioned this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is 10.30. Do you think this would be a convenient moment for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. We are going to have a break now. It is 10.30. We will resume in 25 minutes, that is, at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, when you arrived in Maljine village, you noticed that three houses had been set on fire; whereas, the others were not damaged in any way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You personally didn't know who, when, and how set those three houses on fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you returned to Guca Gora, you have already replied that to my question you learned from a Bosnian Muslim from Krpeljici that it would be good if you went to Bandol village.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You went there and established that the whole village was completely destroyed and that all the houses had been set on fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also established that the local mosque had been completely destroyed. It was beyond recognition. You managed to establish where it had been located, owing to the fact that you had a map of the village.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not entirely true. We managed to find the location of the mosque because the mosque was marked on the map. We did not have a map of the village; simply a map similar to the one I have in front of me now, which showed there to be a mosque in the village, which is why we paid particular attention to locate this building, because it was not obvious when we arrived there where the mosque was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, a mosque was no longer there. It had been razed to the ground. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The -- the building had been completely destroyed and the highest part of the exterior walls of the building would have been only perhaps one, one and a half metres high.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the village, you found a body of a member of the BH army, and there were signs of the previous torture visible on the body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The -- the corpse was half naked. He was wearing trousers and boots, no shirt. He had a -- what looked like a washing line tied around his neck, then. There was evidence of -- that he'd received a severe beating. There was two or three stab wounds in his chest and what looked to me like cigarette burns on his chest. However, the body was in a considerable state of decomposition and it was difficult without medical training to say how long he'd been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, can you please look at the document number 45, dated 13 of June, and can you confirm whether the information that you provided us with about your visit to Guca Gora, about your visit to Maljine and Bandol village, which are all described here under (b), (c), (d), (e), can you confirm that this is exactly what you have testified about today?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not exactly as I've testified, because the -- this milinfosum would have been completed from a variety of sources, then. Not just myself but Randy Rhodes would have had input into this and Captain Mark Bower as well. As I said earlier, I did not notice myself that there had been any evidence of looting in Guca Gora or -- although, as this is written here clearly one of the other members of that patrol did notice this. I did not notice this myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you can confirm that this is a realistic description of the things that you saw, and you can also confirm that this is a milinfosum issued by your battalion.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The milinfosum gives a precis of the -- of the details that -- that we observed on this particular patrol. Clearly it doesn't give every single detail on, this but it is a -- it is a precis of the events that happened on that day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness has confirmed the facts that he's familiar -- that he is familiar with and the fact that this milinfosum was issued by this battalion, I would like this milinfosum to be tendered into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please put your name on this document, sir. But before we admit this document into evidence, I have a question to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, would you please look at item (e) very carefully. Under item (e), you will see the village of Bandol described. The Defence counsel has just asked you a question which is reflected on page 35, line 9. And you replied that you found a body there, the body of a BiH member. In this paragraph (e), is there something here that indicate that this body was the body of a member of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That's absolutely correct, Your Honour. There was no indication that -- that it was a BiH soldier. All I can confirm is that it was a soldier or he was -- or it was -- it was a dead body wearing combat trousers and military boots, then. As to which side he came from, BiH or HVO, it is clearly impossible to say, and that he could have come from either side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. How come that the Defence counsel said in their question that it was the body of a BiH army soldier? What did you base your question on? This was a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as you know, we prepare our questions based on the statements given by the witnesses, and he said in his statement that the village was abandoned and that they discovered the body of a BiH army member. And as the witness said himself, not all the details are recorded in the milinfosums, but I just wanted to confirm that the witness remembers this fact that he mentioned in the statement and he indeed confirmed it before the Trial Chamber with the additional explanation that he gave to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, you said to the investigators of the Tribunal that this was the body of a BiH member. And today you're not absolutely sure about that. Would that be correct to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can clarify this point. The -- we came to the assumption that the body was a BiH soldier based on the following information: First of all, the village was -- was a Muslim village there; secondly, it was surrounded by Croat soldiers. And when we spoke to these Croat soldiers and told them there was a body in the village, they expressed no interest in this whatsoever. We took -- having dealt with the locals before in similar circumstances, they normally took great pains to ensure that their own people were buried. The lack of interest in this particular body led us to the conclusion that he was a member of the opposing forces, i.e., the BiH, which was -- which was the conclusion we came to. But you're absolutely correct, Your Honour, we have no way of knowing which side that body came from for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We are going to give a number to this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number is DH71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, yesterday on direct you said that based on certain suspicions that had come from the HVO and allegations that a crime had been committed in Grahovcici, you decided to visit Grahovcici on the 14th of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, if I may clarify this. I did not decide to go on this patrol. I was tasked by the battalion operations officer to take a United Nations field worker to the village of Grahovcici. Just so the Court understands this, the individual company commanders and patrol commanders did not just decide where they were going to go. The taskings came from the battle group headquarters, then. And although I don't know the exact way that this particular tasking was given, then, it is clear that the initial request came from the United Nations there, which was why they wanted one of their field workers to go to this area to investigate the scene of a possible atrocity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Near Cajdras you were stopped at a checkpoint manned by the BiH army during your mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers there told you that you wouldn't be allowed to go through without a special permit issued by the 3rd Corps Commander.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what they said. They said, "You can't come through without a pass issued by 3 Corps."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, before that, you already knew that the command of the 3rd Corps had issued an order on the free movement of members of the United Nations and other international humanitarian agencies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because of that, you tried to convince the soldiers manning that checkpoint to allow you to go through.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That also is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the soldiers could not be convinced, and you, however, wanted to carry out your mission, you decided to pay a visit to the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: First you met with Mr. Dzemal Merdan, the deputy commander, and then Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic himself.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Commander Hadzihasanovic told you that you did not need any written permits because you had already been granted free passage. However, given the problem that you had encountered, he told you that he would give you some military policemen to escort you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the battalion of the military police of the 3rd Corps was also among those who escorted you; however, at the same checkpoint where you had problems, he also had to argue with the local commander in order to convince him that you should be allowed free passage. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely, again. I don't believe yesterday that I said that the military policeman was the commander of a battalion. I had never seen the man before. He did not introduce himself as a commander of a battalion. As far as I was concerned, he was simply a military policeman, which I believe is what I gave in my evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If there is something else on the record, that may have been a mistake in the interpretation of what you had said; wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe I said that. A -- a battalion commander would imply to me as a military man. This was a senior military policeman in charge of a large number of other military policemen. There was no indication at the time that the military policeman that went with us was anything other than a normal low-ranking policeman. As I said, he did not introduce himself as anything other than a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, the soldier at the checkpoint was not happy. He was actually very angry when he realised that he had to let you through.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry to dispute your exact wording here. I -- I didn't say he was very angry. He was annoyed that we had obtained the military policeman. To my interpretation, "very angry" means -- means exactly those words there. He was annoyed but clearly realised there was nothing he could do about this, which fulfilled our promise to him to do what he asked us to do, and therefore he had no choice but to let us through.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the second checkpoint, although the military policeman insisted on you being let through, it didn't work. They wouldn't let you through, and you had to return to the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, that is, as I believe from my statement yesterday, not exactly what happened there. As I believe I said yesterday, the military policeman enabled us to pass through some other checkpoints, but it was only when we got to Novo Selo that we were stopped at the checkpoints there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that checkpoint - I apologise, I may have been wrong about their numbers - let's say that at that last checkpoint, despite the insistence of the military policeman, you were not allowed to go any further from there.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And the reason that was given to us was that the military policeman could have been a Croat spy and that in any event they were soldiers from a different brigade to the ones which had stopped us at the Cajdras checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your attempt to reach Grahovcici, like on any other occasion, you were able to establish that the real authority lay with the local commanders, local military commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because in this case, when the commander of the checkpoint told me that he was from a different brigade to the ones manning the Cajdras checkpoint, I asked him what brigade he was from and he said 7 Brigade. And I said, "What do I need to get through?" And he said, "I need written authority from the corps commander; otherwise, I will not let you through."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you as a professional soldier must have found it strange that such a high-ranking officer such as the 3rd Corps commander should be involved in the issues that pertained to the authorities of a simple soldier manning a checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did find this surprising. And I mentioned this to the general, and he said that it was because the -- the BiH was still -- still suffering, if you like, from the -- the days of the former Yugoslav National Army when only the man in charge was the one who was able to make decisions. He said that as they were in the middle of a war, it was not possible to change this way but hopefully when the situation was peaceful, they could become more like a -- more like a Western army; for example, the British Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to this question - and I believe that this is very important - it seems to me that you have testified that in the JNA lower-ranking officers could only execute orders that came from their direct superiors.
