In this particular situation that you found yourself in on that particular day, it seems that this soldier, this foot soldier, would only execute orders coming from his direct superior, rather than from the corps commander. The Defence counsel's question was very precise, and you were asked to give a very precise answer. Can you please clarify for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The soldier at the checkpoint said that we could only pass through, that it didn't matter -- let me start again. That he came from a different brigade to the ones at the Cajdras checkpoint, and the only way he would allow us through is if we had a piece of paper from corps headquarters, then, to give him permission. When I spoke to the general, I made -- I made light of this in a -- in a humorous way and said, "If you don't --" words to the effect of, "If you don't mind me saying so, General, it's ridiculous that a man as important as you has to sign this piece of paper to enable me to get through one checkpoint." And that is when he used the analogy of the former Yugoslav National Army to explain why that was the procedure that unfortunately he had to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you informed the general that you hadn't been let through, he was not very happy; he was dissatisfied with the fact that you hadn't been let through the checkpoint. Is that correct? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was clear that he was unhappy that despite having the military policeman, which he had authorised, with us that we had not been allowed through this second checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a professional soldier of a professional army, you must know that the Yugoslav People's Army was a professional army and that it had a very clear system of the unity of command and the way officers communicated amongst each other. I'm sure you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You're also aware of the fact that a corps commander was a high-ranking officer of the Yugoslav People's Army before the war, this particular corps commander.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that a professional soldier would feel embarrassed seeing that his subordinates were not executing orders that he had issued a long time ago?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say that is true, and I believe that to be why the general took time from what must have been a busy day for him to explain to me why this had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because of the fact that his army was being created and found it difficult to follow orders at all times, the general gave you some sort of explanation in order to justify the behaviour of his subordinates; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your patrols in the area of responsibility and your communication with the commanders, you could notice that very often high-ranking officers such as commanders and deputy commanders, together with their soldiers, negotiate things. They didn't issue orders because of the stage of the development of this army, because the unity of command was still not firmly in place. Would I be correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you would be correct. And to further expand on that, another difference between the local forces and, for instance, the British Battalion was an issue of communications. If I wished to speak to my commanding officer, I would simply call him on the radio and talk to him a few moments later. At very few of the checkpoints we went to were there any form of communications. This was before the advent of -- of mass mobile telephones, then, so communications was a problem for both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. During your conversation with General Hadzihasanovic, when you explained the situation with the monastery in Guca Gora, he and his deputy, Merdan, clearly told you that the Mujahedin were not under the control of the BiH army and the 3rd Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I believe in my statement that I said I had this conversation only with Colonel Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you shown a document by which the commander was addressing the staff of the superior command asking them to do something about these foreign soldiers who were out of his control?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall being shown any document to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher to usher [as interpreted] the witness's memory, to show him milinfosum number 46 of the 16th of June, and a document by General Hadzihasanovic dated the 13th of June. And if the witness is able to answer my questions about these documents, I will tender them into evidence. If not, I shall suggest that they be marked for identification. Milinfosums, this one like the others, come from the archives of the British Battalion that we had access to. And General Hadzihasanovic's document was received from the Prosecution, and it is also on the list for General Reinhardt's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The question I put to you has to do with paragraph 1 of this milinfosum. Major, having reviewed this milinfosum, have you been reminded of the conversation that I asked you about, or did you learn subsequently about this at your meeting or, rather, when reading the milinfosum today?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it, the conversation concerning the Mujahedin refers to a conversation between the commanding officer and Colonel Merdan, which took place on the 14th of June, 1993. The conversation between myself and Colonel Merdan took place on a different date, after this milinfosum was issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I only have a few more questions for you. You were finally given a permit and you entered Grahovcici, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, please. We need to clarify a point. The document dated the 14th of June that you have in front of you, and in paragraph 1, under the heading "Meetings," by the way in which it has been drafted, were you referred to in PWO or someone else? Does it apply to someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the expression "CO 1 PWO" specifically refers to the commanding officer, CO being military abbreviation for commanding officer. And what this is saying that Lieutenant Colonel Alastair Duncan today met Enver Hadzihasanovic. This is no reference whatsoever to the conversation that I had with Colonel Merdan at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So you're telling us that the contents of this paragraph does not come from you and that we cannot link this content with the order that you wish to produce, since it doesn't come from the witness. What is actually stated is that it comes from his superior in the hierarchy, and you're telling us that the conversation that you had with Merdan took place before or after the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the 14th, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, after the 14th of June. Very well. Then regarding this document, what is the request of the Defence? That it should be tendered? Placed in standby? In view of the fact that the second document, the order by the general, was something that the witness was not aware of and also this paragraph in the milinfosum was not from him, what is the position of the Defence regarding the two documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to ask a few more questions and then take a position regarding these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, in paragraph 1, in the middle, you can see that the events linked to Guca Gora, in brackets the reference is to milinfosum number 45, which you have recognised as being a part of your information and which has already been admitted into evidence. My question is: The part of the conversation conducted by your commander, were you informed about it at your regular briefing on the same day that the commander had that meeting?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would have been informed of this, and I would have seen this milinfosum. All I'm saying is that in the evidence that I gave, I believe I said that on the 16th of June I had a different conversation with Colonel Merdan, in which he gave me an opposing opinion to the one which is detailed in this milinfosum. And I believe I gave that in evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, Major, if I remember well, your visit to Grahovcici occurred a day after the visit to Guca Gora, which means also on the 14th of June. Am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe you are mistaken. Because if this milinfosum is dated the 14th of June, then milinfosum number 045, the preceding milinfosum, will presumably refer to the events of the 13th of June, then. What this is referring to is my presence at the village of Bandol, then, where it say that is the presence of Warriors prevented 3 Corps from a planned -- or prevented a planned BiH attack. That, I believe, was my vehicles going to the area of Bandol in response to the gentleman who I met in Guca Gora. So the events of this are actually the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for dwelling on this for a moment longer, but if I understand correctly, though a milinfosum is typed the next day but it is dated according to the events that happened on that day, that is, the 14th of June, because through your testimony we have just established that you went to Maljine on the 13th of June, that on the 13th of June you were also in Bandol and Guca Gora, and according to your testimony here in court, on the 14th of June you were tasked to visit Grahovcici. So I assume, Major, that it is possible that the first part of the report contains information from your commander but there is reference also to what you learnt the day earlier visiting Guca Gora and Bandol. Am I interpreting this situation, which is rather complicated, correctly? In view of the fact that in your statement for the Prosecutor and here in court you specifically referred to the 13th when you went to Guca Gora, Maljine, and Bandol, and on the 14th to Grahovcici?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is absolutely correct, ma'am. As I understand this, under the heading "Meetings," paragraph 1, where it says "CO 1 PWO" today met Enver Hadzihasanovic, that event took place on the 14th of June. And the comments made to him at the end of paragraph 1 also took place on that day. During this conversation, it was mentioned that a BiH attack had had to be cancelled due to the president -- due to the presence of Warrior armoured vehicles in Bandol. That, I believe, to be reference to my own presence in Bandol the day before, the 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we've clarified things now. Would you please also look at paragraph 11 of this same milinfosum, and then I will have a couple of questions about it. Actually, you said that when you finally received written permission you managed to pass through this checkpoint as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you finally received this order, you visited the village of Grahovcici as well -- not order, I'm sorry, this permission. Then you managed to enter the village of Grahovcici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in Grahovcici, as well as in Novo Selo, you were obvious -- you were able to see obvious signs of intensive combat?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there was no evidence of ethnic cleansing and the expulsion of Croat inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't reply to that with sufficient detail. All I can say is the person on the ground -- was that there was no evidence that any -- any of the buildings in the village had been burned. I don't believe I'm qualified to comment on whether so-called ethnic cleansing had taken place. All I can say is there were no obvious signs of any buildings being burnt. There was no indication as to what had happened to the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You reported about all this at your regular briefing; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has answered all my questions. In view of the fact that he cannot fully confirm all the facts that took place at the meeting held by his commander, I am suggesting that for the present both documents be marked for identification only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I had intended to ask the Prosecution for their remarks a moment ago. Can we hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we are going to give two numbers to these documents, marked for identification, though milinfosum is an official document. But we will do it on a provisional basis. So please give us two numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the milinfosum will get the exhibit number DH72, marked for identification; the B/C/S version of the report gets the exhibit number DH73, marked for identification; and the English translation of the report gets the exhibit number DH73/E, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for this witness. Major, thank you very much for the answers you have given me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now turn to the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will have a few questions for this witness, and they will refer exclusively to what the witness has been saying before this Chamber yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, in the course of your testimony yesterday and today, you spoke about your own experiences during your tour of duty in Central Bosnia in 1993. You stayed in Central Bosnia, according to your own statement, from April 1993 until the 31st of August, when you were transferred to Tuzla; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct, sir. I believe I stated in my statement that I spent -- that I spent the whole time of the tour as -- as the Vitez company commander. What I believe I said was that "A" Company and the Light Dragoon's Squadron swapped over the duties in Tuzla. I myself didn't go to Tuzla at any point during the tour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: So you were in Central Bosnia throughout your tour of duty in Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony, Major, you spoke about your experiences and your mission during your stay in Central Bosnia. Among other things, as you yourself described yesterday and also today, you had some direct contact with foreign fighters, the Mujahedin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your first contact, according to your testimony, was on the 15th of May, 1993 near the village of Fazlici.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You were surprised, as you yourself said, before -- because before that you had absolutely no awareness of the existence of these foreign combatants in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You described your meeting with them in detail, and you told us that it lasted roughly between one and two hours at that checkpoint at Fazlici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, there were no local soldiers with these foreigners who described them as plastic Mujahedins, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I believe I testified that there were two groups of soldiers there: Ones who were clearly local militia, and ones who were foreigners. I do not believe that I said there were any of the so-called plastic Mujahedin there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your second encounter with these foreign combatants was on the 13th of June, 1993 in Guca Gora, when you were on your way to the village of Maljine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You went to the village of Maljine under Mujahedin escort, as you said. There were three foreign fighters with you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In your escort, there were no soldiers of the BH army on that occasion, were there?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th of June, 1993, according to your own testimony, after receiving all the necessary permits and after describing to us how all this happened, you were stopped -- I'm sorry, let me rephrase my question. On the 14th of June, 1993, when you were on your way to Grahovcici, you were stopped at a BH army checkpoint at a place called Novo Selo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In order to pass through that checkpoint, you were required to get appropriate passes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You learnt at the checkpoint that these were members of the 7th Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you noticed some soldiers who were imitating the foreign fighters in the way they dressed and in their appearance, and it was then that you described them as so-called plastic Mujahedin, but in fact they were all Bosniaks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your own assessment that these were local soldiers and Bosniaks, the appearance of the plastic Mujahedin for people who were not familiar to the same extent as you were with the situation could lead somebody to conclude that they were foreign soldiers.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you're asking me to comment on other people's opinions. However, I believe that from a distance to an untrained eye, yes, there could be perhaps some form of -- some form of dispute as to the actual -- the actual ethnic group these people came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: After you acquired the pass from the 3rd Corps, you went to Grahovcici unhindered; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You inferred and learnt that they were members of the 7th Brigade because that is what they themselves said; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The date is indeed the 14th of June, 1993, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is -- if that is what I gave on my statement, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On the day you arrived in Grahovcici, you did not notice any damage or burnt houses, except that you did see traces of heavy fighting, as you yourself said.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that to be the case either. I believe what I said was that there was some damage to the buildings which was consistent with them having been shelled; however, there was no signs that buildings had been set on fire deliberately as a means of simply destroying the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Major, do you know that on the 11th of June, 1993 a battle started with units of the HVO in the environs of Kakanj and in the town of Kakanj itself?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall this incident because that was outside our -- our own battle group's area; however, if this incident took place, it is likely that we would have been briefed on that in the evening briefing as an event of interest taking place in a neighbouring battle group's area. Although, I'm afraid I do not recall any details of this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, during your tour of duty in Central Bosnia, you never met Mr. Kubura, the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Central Bosnia, you never went to the headquarters of the 7th Muslim Brigade either; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And during that period of time, you had no other contact with any high-ranking officer of the 7th Muslim Brigade, did you?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Your only contact with members of the 7th Brigade was the one you described on the 14th of June, 1993 at the checkpoint in Novo Selo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that with any degree of certainty. What I can say is the only time that I met a soldier who positively identified himself as a member of 7 Muslim Brigade was on the incident which I've described on the 14th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Major, during your testimony yesterday, in answer to questions from the President you discussed how information was collected which you used during your mission.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you indicated that one of the very important segments of data collection was the information you gathered from the locals of the villages that were inhabited by Croat farmers. This is something you confirmed today during the cross-examination. And you also referred to elderly people, civilians, who were living in those villages as a source of information. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry again to pick words with you, sir. I do not believe I mentioned the words -- the word "Croat farmers" in my testimony yesterday. And when I gave my testimony, I believe that I made it clear that the information-gathering process was the same for any villages, be they Muslim or Croat, that we went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, they were local inhabitants of the villages from which you collected information, be they Croat or Muslim villages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Major, would you agree with me when I say that the information that the local population had about the military situation and the situation on the ground was absolutely limited and sometimes very superficial? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The amount of information that we were given varied in quality. Sometimes it was clearly true. And by that, it would be something that we had intimate knowledge of ourselves. Sometimes it was blatantly false and simply propaganda. And sometimes it was somewhere in the middle, due to the informant being -- not having full possession of all the factors, though, which was why we took every step to corroborate any information that we were given from either other sources or, if possible, independent sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you gave us some examples of what happened during your mission, when the mission could not be accomplished fully because of the information that was incomplete. For example, when you went to Maljine, you used a map that was carried by Mr. Bower and that map was absolutely incorrect; it was incomplete. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say the map was incomplete. I said the map had no scale and no north pointer on it, so therefore was impossible to orientate with any recognisable feature in the village of Maljine. To the person that drew that map, it may have been useful. But to us, as a third party, trying to make use of that in this particular village, indeed it was useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the information that you had received, you didn't find any traces of crime in Grahovcici village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony yesterday, you said that the UN camp was only 2 kilometres away from Ahmici village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, I don't believe I said that. I said "several kilometres." I do not believe I specified the distance 2, 2 kilometres, because I know that to be incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's agree that it was several kilometres. However, despite the fact that it was only several kilometres away, you had no information whatsoever of what would happen in Ahmici village and subsequently you also didn't have any information as to who had committed the crime or who had ordered the crime to be committed.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only comment on my own views and observations of this tour. The events in Ahmici took place before I deployed to Bosnia, so the -- the feelings and actions of the British troops at that time must be commented on by someone who was there at the time. I believe I testified that at the time that we arrived in Bosnia it was unclear who had carried out the atrocity and why, and this was the subject of an investigation which was ongoing when we arrived out in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Major, during your testimony yesterday, you confirmed that you had already given a statement to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You gave this statement on the 10th of May, 2000 in the presence of Mr. Hackshaw and Mr. Stephan Obers, both of them investigators of The Hague Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you spoke about the same events that you spoke about yesterday and today before this Trial Chamber; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. No, I would like to -- I would like to change that. That is not correct. I spoke about the -- the parts of my tour which I was asked questions about by the -- by the investigators. For instance, I did not make as many comments about the -- the visit to the village of Bandol. I made these observations and comments in response to -- to questions posed to me by the Defence. These were not part of my statement. At the time, I simply answered questions which were given to me in this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I please ask the usher to give the major the statement that he gave to the investigators in the year 2000, because I will have some questions that stem from that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Major, is this the statement that you gave to the investigators and signed yourself?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the last page of that statement. It says here that the statement has been read over to you in the English language, which is your mother tongue, and that this statement is true. So is this correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And you signed every single page of this statement.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 9, line 6, starting with "From my observation in Central Bosnia." You say clearly in this statement that you cannot confirm whether the Mujahedin were involved or included in the 7th Muslim Brigade or not.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When you gave this statement to the investigators, you used your own log or your own diary.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Major, based on what you have said today about your contacts - namely, you stated that you didn't have any contacts with the high-ranking officers of the Muslim -- 7th Muslim Brigade and that the only contact that you had with that brigade was at Grahovcici checkpoint on the 14th of June - one may conclude that your knowledge and your information about the structure of this brigade, of the 7th Brigade, is not sufficient. I'm talking about your personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct. In order to -- to gain the British Battalion's detailed knowledge of the 7th Brigade, you would need to speak to the particular liaison officer who was involved in frequent contact with 7 Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. But before I do so, I'm wondering to what purpose the Defence for Mr. Kubura was going to use this statement of the witness, whether that needs to be withdrawn from the witness or whether -- what their intention is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we do not tender this statement into evidence. We just wanted the witness to have it and to refer to it when we were checking the witness's credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. President, perhaps that statement should be withdrawn from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, I just have a few questions for you. In response to a question put to you by Mrs. Residovic, in the transcript today, page 44, line 8, you indicated that you were aware that the accused Hadzihasanovic was a high-ranking officer of the JNA before the war. Do you remember saying that this morning?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, we were given personality briefs of the major commanders, then, and part of this included what -- what prior military experience they had received. To give you some examples that I can recall, General Hadzihasanovic had previous experience in the -- in the JNA; General Alagic had been a tank commander; on the Croat side, Brigadier Vlado Juric had been the pilot of a ground-attack aircraft. So we were given this information to enable us to assess the actions of the various combatants, some of whom had no senior military experience but were simply local commanders because of their esteemed position within society, not necessarily because they were efficient military soldiers in a previous life. So we were briefed that. But I'm afraid I can't recall any document that said that on; merely the fact that I remember that I was told that in a briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major, do you recall from that briefing any of the specific experience of General Hadzihasanovic in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid I do not, other than the fact that he had been a reasonably high-ranking officer. And by that I took that to mean of around the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would ask that the witness be shown DH71.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, I just have a couple of questions regarding the technical format, if you will, of the milinfosum infosums of which DH71 is an example. At the top of this document, the first line, the line that's underscored says "1 PWO." Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that abbreviation stands for?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to 1st Battalion, the Prince of Wales' Own Regiment of Yorkshire, which is the United Kingdom battle Group to which -- of which I was a member of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you look at the first paragraph, paragraph number 1, the final sentence of that paragraph there is an abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about "C/S"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this means "call sign." By "call sign," it's a military euphemism for patrol. Each patrol -- each vehicle has a different call sign painted on the side of the turret to enable easy identification of one's own vehicle and also to enable the local people should they be reporting any actions carried out by the United Nations to ensure that they would be able to recognise the vehicle and that the battalion hierarchy would then be able to know which vehicle was involved in any particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, if you know, can you please describe for the Trial Chamber how the milinfosums are physically produced; that is, are they prepared on a typewriter or a computer or any other type of -- of machinery? Do you know -- if you know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't know exactly how the milinfosum was produced, whether it was done -- whether it was typed or done on computer. I was not involved with the production of this. My only involvement with milinfosums would be to physically give my written patrol report, which would generally be handwritten, to a member of the military information cell, and they would collate that information and produce a milinfosum similar to the one I have in front of me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your indulgence, I would ask that the usher briefly escort the witness out of the courtroom. I would like to address the Chamber in his absence before asking the final one or two questions that I have for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In the cross-examination conducted by Defence for Mr. Kubura, the witness obviously was shown his prior OTP statement. The Prosecution submits that the question that was put to the witness was an entirely proper question by the Defence; however, the -- the part of the sentence from his statement that was put to the witness was only part of that sentence from his witness statement. In light of the Trial Chamber's prior rulings with respect to the use of written witness statements by the Prosecution, prior to proceeding I thought it was prudent to seek the Trial Chamber's guidance. What I am proposing to do is to put the entire sentence that is in the witness' statement to him. This would be the complete sentence of which my learned colleague for the Defence put only a part of that sentence to him. And I would propose to proceed in the following way: By simply reading the entire sentence as contained in the witness statement to the witness and asking him whether or not to the best of his recollection that is an accurate and truthful sentence from his statement. And I simply do that in the absence of the witness to seek guidance of the Chamber, in light of the prior rulings with respect to use of prior statements by the Prosecution. And that would, in fact, be my last question for the witness. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, we have to make a break. We are thus going to make a break, and we shall give you our reply after this break. However, Mr. Bourgon would like the floor for an intervention. Before we give him the floor, we need to say that the document that was given to the witness was something that he read. He familiarised himself with this paragraph of the statement. And now the Prosecution is asking whether they can remind the witness of the entire paragraph. So the goal was to remind the witness of the entire paragraph. However, since the witness was faced with the document, he read it, and this was already resolved. But we will talk about it and we will reply. Mr. Bourgon, you wanted the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The question that was put about this document was a very precise answer that called for a very precise fact. The re-examination has to be limited to what was said during the cross-examination. And if the Trial Chamber allows the witness to go beyond that, at that moment the Defence is going to ask to be able to put additional questions based on the witness's answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. That goes without saying. Mr. Dixon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. In our submission, there's no need for the witness to be shown his statement again. It wasn't exhibited, the statement. He was shown it in order to answer a particular question, which we put. We only put that question because it was raised in the examination-in-chief yesterday. He had ample opportunity to -- to read the entire paragraph. In fact, he was referred to the entire paragraph. He took his time and he answered the question. And we believe the matter has now been dealt with and there's no need for the statement to be shown again to the -- the witness in re-examination. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Mundis. But when the witness was given the document, he read the paragraph in question. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In fact, if you -- if Your Honours during the break would take a look at the precise question that was put to the witness, the Prosecution would submit that's why he gave a very precise answer to that question. I think over the past two days we've seen that this witness tends to answer questions quite precisely, and in light of the fact that it was a very precise question and it related only to the 7th Muslim Brigade and the Mujahedin, he then didn't elaborate or provide any additional information, which the Prosecution asserts is in his statement. It is precisely for that reason, the precise nature of the question, that the Prosecution would submit that he gave the precise answer that he did in fact give. We should also, in our submission, Your Honour, again, in light of the Chamber's prior ruling on the use of -- of previously given written statements, the Prosecution would submit that it -- that it is proper when the Defence puts questions to witnesses based on the statement that if they don't read directly out of the statement and read completely from the statement that the Chamber in fact might get -- might be -- not have the full picture with respect to what the witness said because the Chamber does not have the written witness statements in front of them. And finally, Your Honours, with respect to the submissions of my -- my learned colleague Mr. Dixon, I -- I again stress we have no intention of showing the witness his statement. We would simply read one sentence from that statement to the witness and ask him to verify whether or not that full sentence, a part of which the Defence put to him, is in fact accurate and true to the best of his recollection sitting here today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Your Honours, since we are discussing this issue in the absence of the witness - and we believe that this is a good procedure to follow - maybe my learned friend could explain what kind of questions he wants to put to the witness. We want to be advised in order to prepare ourselves for possible objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe to avoid wasting time, maybe Mr. Mundis would be able to tell us what lines he wants to read in the presence of the witness. Without that, maybe we are just beating around the bush. Maybe you can explain and tell us what line, what sentences, what words you would like to read to the witness, and then we will all listen to this sentence with a lot of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it comes from the sixth paragraph on page 9, which is precisely the paragraph that Mr. Ibrisimovic referred the witness to. It is the second and final sentence of that paragraph, and the question that I would propose putting to the witness is the following: Major Kent-Payne, in your statement of 10 May 2000 did you tell the investigators of the Tribunal the following: "I cannot, however, say whether the Mujahedin were attached to or under the control of the 7th Muslim Brigade directly or that they reported directly to the 3rd Corps Command"? Sir, did you in fact make that statement and sitting here today is it a true and accurate statement to the best of your recollection? That, Mr. President, is the precise question that the Prosecution would like to put to the witness. If you compare the previous question asked by the Defence with the question that the Prosecution would propose, both of which come from his prior statement, the Prosecution submits it will be clear to Your Honours precisely why that question is relevant and why that question would be of great assistance to the Trial Chamber as it makes determinations as to the ultimate issues involved in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we know exactly what needs to be clarified about this statement given in May 2000. Does the Defence still object to the reading of this sentence which basically arises logically from the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to reply to my learned friend. My learned friend said that my question was precise and that I obtained a very precise answer. I believe that this is the goal of the procedure before this Trial Chamber. I limited my question to what the Defence of Mr. Kubura is interested in, because he was the commander of the 7th Brigade, and we obtained a precise answer. I did not ask any questions with regard to the subordination to the 3rd Corps, and I believe that no such question can be asked during re-examination, because I never asked any questions about the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Mundis, because the discussion is getting really interesting. The Defence tells us that they asked the witness whether the Mujahedin had been subordinated to the 7th Brigade. The witness answered that he couldn't answer that question. The Prosecution would now like to complete this question by asking the witness whether he had said that he couldn't reply whether they were subordinated to the 7th Brigade or not; however, in the written statement, he also added to that that he also wouldn't be able to say whether they were directly subordinated to the 3rd Corps command. So this is the gist of the debate. You want the witness to give us his opinion as to the subordination to the 3rd Corps. And the Defence objects to that. Am I -- am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, the -- the question -- and we're not suggesting in any way whatsoever that the question as put by my learned colleague Mr. Ibrisimovic is improper or incorrect. Clearly if I were sitting on that side of the courtroom I would be asking exactly the same question. If you look at his question, page 60, line 2 of today's transcript, and compare that with what's contained in the witness's actual statement, as reflected by the proposed question which I just put to you, which was a direct quote from his statement, you will see that the issue is exactly as Your Honour has put it, that the precise question that was put to the witness resulted in a very precise answer but the witness was not then asked to go further. And the Prosecution would assert that comparing what he actually said in his prior written statement with the question -- the precise question that was put to him today could result in a situation where the Trial Chamber does not have all the information which the -- which the Prosecution submits it should have and which this witness can testify to. That -- that, again, Mr. President, you've got the precise question that I would put to the witness, and those are the submissions on this issue for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I'm going to give the floor to Mr. Bourgon. But before that, I would like to summarise. The Prosecution says that the Defence has asked a certain question. I can see it on the record on page 60, line 2 and further on. And the Defence has asked the witness whether he was able to confirm that the -- as it says in the statement, that the Mujahedin were a part of the 7th Brigade. The witness then replied that he was not in the position to answer that question. The Prosecution submits that this question was asked in such a way that the real situation was not represented in the -- the proper way, because what the witness stated in his statement is said in such a way that one could infer that there was a link with the 3rd Corps. This is something that should not be discussed in such a narrow sense. He has to be given an opportunity to say what he meant when he gave his answer. Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position of the Defence is very clear. When the witness was asked a precise question, he gave a very precise answer. And in that he had the entire statement in front of him. And now the question that the Prosecution wants to put to the witness now has already been put to the question during the examination-in-chief. This issue was already the subject of our previous discussion. And -- and the questions that were put to the witness by the Trial Chamber -- the question put to the witness by the Trial Chamber was what sources he had at his disposal when he put his positions forward. So the Defence believes that if the Prosecutor is allowed to ask this question, this will mean that they will be allowed to put a question that doesn't stem from the cross-examination of this witness. The Trial Chamber will do what they deem necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. It is twenty-five to 1.00. We will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. The Chamber deliberated the question whether the Prosecution could put a question to the witness on the basis of the paragraph contained in his written statement, the Chamber, referring to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which allows parties to ask questions upon authorisation of the Chamber, the Chamber authorises this question to be asked. Mr. Mundis, you may put the question to the witness, referring to the content of the said paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Major Kent-Payne, in your statement of 10 May 2000, did you tell the investigators of the Tribunal the following: "I cannot, however, say whether the Mujahedin were attached to or under the control of the 7th Muslim Brigade directly or that they reported directly to the 3rd Corps Command"? Sir, did you in fact make that statement, and sitting here today, is it a true and accurate statement to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I believe I meant by that statement, in answer to the question that was posed, was could I confirm that the -- that the Mujahedin were attached to any particular organisation. And I answered in my opinion truthfully that I could not confirm that that was the case. I took that to be that confirmation would be, had I seen any members of the Mujahedin in 3 Corps headquarters, for instance, which to my mind will be evidence, which I do not believe that I had seen, so I answered that I could not confirm this. I believe earlier on in my statement I was asked my opinion on this, and I said that we were told in a briefing that this was the -- was the organisation. But in answer to the exact wording of my statement, no, I could not confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I guess, sir, my question was: Did you say that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Kent-Payne.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges have some questions for you, so, Witness, please listen carefully to the questions, as you have done over the past two days, and you will give us precise answers. So I give the floor to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Major. I would like to put to you a few questions about mainly the matter of destruction of houses. You have talked about it and I would like to have some clarifications on that issue. You told us that the first time you wanted to visit Guca Gora was on the day of the attack. What you said yesterday was that BritBat, your company, wanted to prevent a second Ahmici, so to speak, and you also were interested in -- you had a policy, you said yesterday, if I quote you correctly, of investigating the burning of houses. That was a very short remark. And my first question is: What did this policy contain? What did you mean by that statement?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant that if we were on a routine patrol and we saw a house burning, then we were, in our opinion, duty-bound to investigate that if at all possible. By that I mean driving to the location to see if we could help anyone perhaps trapped inside the building or prevent any -- anyone being killed by -- by whoever had set fire that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So that implies that you are patrolling in a certain area and whenever there is a question or you see a house burning or if there is something else that attracts your attention, you investigate the matter.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Because we were given a considerable degree of latitude to use our initiative, then, and this was one item where individual patrol commanders were told, "If you are going from point A to point B and you see this happening and if at all possible, then you are to investigate." An example where it would not be possible to investigate would be if -- if a patrol commander was escorting a convoy and clearly his primary mission is to get that convoy from A to B safely. And what he would then do is radio back to the United Nations base and if possible another patrol would be sent to investigate the burning building or the sound of firing or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. So this is basically reactive. You are on patrol, and then you are confronted with certain phenomenon.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I had yesterday and also this morning a slightly different impression. This is my second question to you: You could also imagine a policy of -- following the events consisting of visiting place where fights have been -- where fights have occurred and on a regular basis visiting those places and see what are the differences in -- in the environment. Have new houses been burnt? Have new houses been destroyed, et cetera? But that was not your policy.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a question of policy, Your Honour. It's a question of gaining information. So to go to one village that had been taken over by a particular side, then -- and then perhaps if we visited that village a week later, part of the information that we would send back was that there'd clearly been looting, the windows in the church were smashed, there was three houses burned down, there was a large quantity of refugees that moved into this area, and all that would be information that we would pass back to our -- to our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So the first time you wanted to go to Guca Gora and you said "We have a policy of investigating the burning of houses," then that day you did not succeed in reaching Guca Gora. You were turned back, and the next day you returned, and then to -- you got involved in the evacuation of the -- the Croatian civilians in the monastery.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. But on the first day, there were actually soldiers from my battalion but from the operations company stationed in Guca Gora, and they were -- they, as part of their -- their interpretation of the scene, took all the civilians from the village and put them for safekeeping in the monastery, and it then took, as it -- as it transpired, approximately 24 hours to actually organise the relief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: All right. That's what you said also yesterday. But when you came the second day, you yourself succeeded in reaching Guca Gora and evacuating the Croatians in the monastery there, which took quite a while. I think you thought -- said it took about -- a process of some hours.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And you also said there was some fighting going on, some shooting. What did you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that, I mean there was shooting going on which was close enough to be concerned about but not close enough to react to. So there were clearly hostile forces - by that I mean hostile to each other, as opposed to necessarily hostile to us - in the area, and the presentation of a large target, in this case a large number of civilians, could well have made whoever was attacking then decide to do something about this, which was why we -- we picked a route which was covered to move these people from the doors of the monastery into the vehicles and why we only filled one vehicle at a time. Had we just been able to take all the people outside of the monastery and put into vehicles at the same time, the whole operation would have only taken half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Yes. Did you see any fighting yourself?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this particular day, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: No. And one of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day before, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I mean in the process of evacuation.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not see any fighting as such, no, because -- because the presence of our vehicles and the presence of the other companies' Warriors in a defensive perimeter around this part of the village prevented any ingress by the attacking forces into the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: What did you -- did you -- make you think that was there was a fight? There was firing, of course, but was there a fight between parties?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the evidence of listening to the radio traffic of the day before, when what is called a contact report - a contact report is a report sent to the headquarters of the battalion giving the facts that rounds have been returned and giving details of the target and the result of the rounds being fired at the target, in this case casualties on the attacking -- the attack forces. And so although I did not see it personally, I was able to hear the shooting and identify the difference between our own vehicle shooting and the -- and the opposition shooting and draw my conclusions from that. And also, from talking to the soldiers, who we relieved at the monastery the day I arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at that moment, on that day or any of your -- your subordinates or colleagues in the same group you were in do any investigation into the burning of houses or the destruction of houses?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- our main mission for this particular operation was to evacuate the -- the people from the monastery, then, and that was simply what we did. There was no scope for -- for moving outside. And as -- as militia forces had clearly shot at our own soldiers, and if you're shot at, then there's clearly an intent to harm, then it was -- it was not worth moving outside the cleared perimeter in order to investigate any other buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You say militia building -- people shot at us. What kind of militia was that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the reports that -- that I heard over the radio, these were -- these were foreigners, people of Arabic or coloured origin, then, as identified through the powerful gunnery sight of the Warriors that were stationed in the -- in the square of the monastery at Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And at that day when you went to Guca Gora or crossed Guca Gora or came back from Guca Gora, did you see any houses burning?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my -- to my recollection, no. But if I can clarify that, at this stage there had clearly been a major offensive carrying on, and it would not have been unusual to -- for there to be houses burning, then. But as I say, our primary mission was to -- to escort those people to the safety of the -- of the refugee centre for the Croats in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Then you went back on the 13th, I think. We have discussed that matter in relation to a milinfosum, number 45, and you said this morning - and this is also in the -- in this report of your unit - there was evidence of looting but there had been no attempts to destroy formerly Croat houses. And you confirmed that this morning also, I think. How did you come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I believe I said earlier, sir, I -- I don't believe that I made the statements for this milinfosum there, that there was evidence of looting. I do not remember seeing that. But what I can confirm is that the -- that the -- the houses in the village had not been burned, then, and I used my experiences of at that stage of witnessing Ahmici and how a concerted effort had been made by local forces to physically destroy the village and this had not taken place in -- in Guca Gora at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: When you write down something like the following: "There has been no attempt to destroy formerly Croat houses," that could mean that you have not seen at the moment you were there any attempt at destructing --

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: -- houses.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: So from our position -- and bear in mind we did not leave the road at any stage then. So from my position on that road, I could not see either any houses burning or any burnt houses in -- in that location. Clearly I could not confirm what went on after I left. But my view at the time was that the village was largely intact and the only damage was -- was what I would call collateral battle damage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And how many houses would this concern, then?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't recall the exact number, but there had been -- when our "A" Company were in the -- in the village, there had been some firing at them, some firing of small mortar rounds, rocket-propelled grenades. And while they won't normally destroy a house, they will -- they will put in windows, make small holes in the roof, and cause shrapnel damage. Only on certain occasions would the hot shrapnel from such devices set fire to the house. And it's -- it's fairly easy to tell whether a house has physically been set on fire or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: What's the difference? Can you still explain it maybe?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously I'm not a fireman, sir, but -- but a -- a house which is set on fire deliberately normally starts burning at the bottom and then the flames go upwards and the last thing to disappear is the roof. A house that has been set on fire by a direct hit from shell fire normally starts burning from the top floor and then burns down to the bottom, then, because the explosion has been on the top floor or inside the roof space, then. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The final result may be the same, or is that not so?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The final result would be exactly the same, a burned-out shell of a building, yes. That's absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you're also saying, if I understand you well the sort of weaponry was not heavy enough to destroy a house directly.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sorts of weaponry that was used on this particular occasion in the attack against Guca Gora from this -- my conversations with soldiers who were there at that time - and there were no heavy weapons, by that I mean heavy artillery used in that attack and therefore there would not have been buildings destroyed by those weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So returning back to your statement on the 13th, when you have said and it was also said in the milinfosum "Have not been any attempts to destroy formerly Croatian houses," that does not cover only your -- the moment of your presence but goes back to the whole period before you came; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. So there were no what I would call burned-out buildings, buildings that had been on fire but were no longer burning. If there were, I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. When you came back another time - I think, if I'm correct, the day after that, the 14th or maybe the 15th - and you then went to the church. You visited the church.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You saw some harm having been done to the church, broken windows, Arabic texts, et cetera. And I take it you reported that also in one of these milinfosums.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you also write a report or any other colleague of yours on the church, on the situation in the church?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, I would have made a written patrol report, which would have been handed in to the military information cell for them to -- for them to collate and to put if they saw fit onto the milinfosum examples of which we've seen here. Clearly those documents are -- are just that, a document, then, and every single item that was reported would not normally be put on there. And it was a valued judgement made by the military information officer as to what went on on these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did these reports sometimes go higher up, to -- to --

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not sometimes. Sir, they should have always gone up to the -- to the brigade headquarter, which was down in Split, and almost certainly to the United Nations local headquarters, which was in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The United Nations, your central command in Split, other -- European Union maybe?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The British command was in Split. So our immediate British commander was the -- was the -- the UNPROFOR British brigadier and was based down in Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Were such reports also sent to -- to local authorities, to the HVO or to the commanders of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, with respect, this is outside of my pay grade and knowledge, but I would not imagine that that would be the case. These were military -- by the mere term "military information summary," milinfosum, would be for the -- the digestion of military personnel, be they from the British Battalion, the British High Command headquarters, indeed our own military defence, and also the UN military headquarters as well. If there was any sharing of this informs, I do not imagine it would have gone down any further than perhaps the -- the UNHCR, certainly not to the locals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: At this moment, when you visited the church and saw the camouflage damage done to the interior of the building, did you have a look also at the situation in Guca Gora? Did you again look at the damage done to houses?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so much damage done to houses, but I did notice outside the church that the graves of the Croats who had been killed in the fighting and had been buried by our regimental padre had been desecrated. The simple home-made wooden crosses which had been put on the graves had been pulled out of the ground and smashed up, and that I did notice. I did not notice that there had been more recent burnings of houses within the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And then I understand you once more visited Guca Gora at the end of June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You saw some improvement on the interior of the church. You saw that -- that the church was cleaned and then --

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a group of -- a group of middle-aged and elderly women there cleaning up the church under the supervision of a BiH military policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: This would have been some two weeks after the former visit.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you notice any change in the situation as far as the houses were concerned?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall if that was the case. What I do remember is that people were moving into the area and that looting was taking place. And this was a common occurrence. And to be honest, something that we would barely bother to report there, because as soon as -- as soon as inhabitants ran out -- ran away from their buildings, then within a very short space of time looting would take place indeed from all sides, though it was not confined to any one particular side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have indicated that you -- when you went to Guca Gora there were three journalists who were with you, one of whom was a cameraman. And these journalists, did they come upon the initiative of your commander, at the initiative of the UN, or were they journalists who sort of self-invited themselves?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if I may bore you with a slightly explanation of this -- of this matter. At the initial part of our tour of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the journalists, of which there were a large number due to the international, particularly Western European interest in the situation, would travel around in their own vehicles, sometimes with United Nations vehicles but other times on their own, in order to get their stories. Then it became the situation that the HVO, the Croat militia, then started to believe that the slant that the media was placing on their television and newspaper reports was biassed towards the him side and biassed against the Croat side. So they therefore made threats that they would kill any members of the media who they -- who they would find going about their duties. It therefore transpired that the United Nations headquarters issued a directive that in order to facilitate the -- the gathering of media stories, that the media organisations would be pooled together and that these would be tasked on United Nations patrols by the public information officer, in our case Major James Miles. A pool system meant that you could perhaps have a French cameraman, a BBC news reporter, and an Italian newspaper reporter. And at the end of the day, they would pool their stories together and each television channel would use the -- the footage taken by the lone cameraman. So the -- the presence of the press was not on my own initiative, it was not on their initiative; it was on the initiative of the -- of the United Nations press information officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You also said that before taking up your duties on the ground you were in Germany, where you had a briefing on the situation from your colleagues who were there before you. And during those briefings, did they ever mention the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they were not mentioned to us at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In the mission of which you were a part, and at first one understood it was to escort a humanitarian convoy, but later on your mission went beyond that and you accomplished other tasks as well. You said that you also participated in prisoner exchange. Did you personally participate in prisoner exchanges as a representative of your own military unit and under the auspices of the UN?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Do you wish me to describe -- to describe an example, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please give us an example.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: One example was I was tasked to go to the village of Prustica [phoen], which is to the south of Vitez, which was a Muslim-held visit -- village, and to negotiate the release of three Croat prisoners, then, who were being held in a -- an iso-container, by that I mean a metal container of the sort that would be carried on the back of a lorry. And I believed when I arrived there that these people would be soldiers, but in fact they turned out to be middle aged to elderly men who had simply been working in their fields and had been captured. And their release was secured by a representative of the International Commission of the Red Cross and we carried these people into the Croat area of Vitez and then simply let them go, and the representative of the Red Cross ensured that they returned back to their houses. That is one such example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A final question for me - and Madam Judge to my right has a question for you too - but my last question: You explained to us that when you were at the checkpoint you were not allowed to pass and you had to go to the headquarters to obtain that famous pass. Within the logic of your mission, which was to move freely on the whole territory, and there was only a single soldier and yet you were in a vehicle which provided protection, why did you go back to ask for a pass when you could have easily passed a single soldier even if he were to open fire at your vehicle, it wouldn't cause much damage, because your vehicle was probably armoured. Why did you go back to ask for this pass? Could you explain that for us, please.

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our instructions were very clear, Your Honour, that we were not to become the -- in our area the third force in the conflict, then. So by "third force" I mean the BiH, the HVO, and the United Nations. And our instructions were very clear to wherever possible avoid damaging any -- any property. And by that we were instructed that that meant the fabric of a checkpoint, then, and that the way to get through checkpoints was by negotiation or if it was particularly important in the case of the escort, this UN worker, by obtaining the piece of paper that would be required to fulfil our mission. Yes, of course we could have easily driven over the checkpoint and absorbed any small arms ammunition, but that was not why we were there and that would be provocation, then. And the next time we went to that checkpoint and needed to go through, then clearly we -- the -- the checkpoint would be mined with anti-tank mines and we would have even more difficulty. We tried to be as -- as conciliatory as possible with the local militias in order to make things as easy as possible for the -- for any troops that went to the checkpoint on a subsequent day. We were there to -- to keep the peace, to escort convoys, not to enforce the peace by becoming involved as -- as peacemakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
