utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In view of the fact that we have posed additional questions, do the parties wish to ask the witness to clarify any points stemming from the questions that we put to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His Honour Judge Swart asked you about some more detailed information about the burning of houses in Guca Gora and about what you saw. Please tell me: Is it true that on the 7th of June on the radio and the other media as well - and also, this could be visualised in the Bila Valley - that there was smoke seen in the area of Guca Gora? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's entirely possible, given the facts that -- that small-calibre mortars were being fired and indeed that other activities were taking place in that area. It's entirely possible that some buildings were being burned; although, I did not see that myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that UNPROFOR units, your colleagues from other units, representatives of the European Community and representatives of the army went to check whether the monastery in Guca Gora had been set on fire because the Croatian media brought stories about the monastery being set on fire? Are you aware of the fact?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm well aware of that fact, which was why I personally was tasked to accompany the regimental padre and the priest -- the Croat priest from Vitez to the monastery. As I recall, I was on guard duty at this time and would not normally have been required to do this, but the commanding officer asked me to go myself, as perhaps the person who knew more about the situation within that monastery and -- than anyone else. And the sole reason for this visit was to show the priest there that the damage had been conducted inside the monastery but that contrary to the rumours which you mentioned, the monastery had not been burned down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the investigations that were subsequently carried out proved that the fire and smoke that could be seen above Guca Gora was actually smoke that came from Bandol village, that was indeed burnt down, rather than from the monastery?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is entirely possible, if the observer was a -- was either not familiar with the area or had not got the ability to look closely with, for instance, binoculars there. It is entirely possible that smoke from Bandol, which is to the south of Guca Gora, could be interpreted by someone much further to the south, then, as coming from -- from Guca Gora. That's -- that's my opinion. I was not there, but that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, you have provided a detailed answer as to what damages you see in Guca Gora as a result of war operations in Guca Gora, in Novo Selo, and in Grahovcici. In response to a question by the Honourable Judge, you said that you had had a previous experience with Ahmici. Can you please tell us what you saw as war damages in Guca Gora, Novo Selo, and in Grahovcici was -- was it anything like what you saw in Ahmici or anything like what you see in Bandol village?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Completely different. The -- the situations in Ahmici and Bandol, there had clearly been an attempt to systematically destroy, in the case of Bandol, the whole village; in the case of Ahmici, the houses which had previously been occupied by Muslims, then. That is to say, not every house in Ahmici had been destroyed. There were some which were occupied by Croat families that had not been -- not been destroyed by fire in the same way. The damage that I witnessed in Grahovcici, Novo Selo, and Guca Gora was that, in my opinion, was consistent with -- with battle damage and -- and perhaps looting but not as a concerted effort to burn the whole village down. I did not see that at any time in any of those three villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, to a question put to you by the Honourable Judge, you have also said that later on, which was customary after war operations, there was some looting, some plunder, even large-scale looting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The looting would -- that we witnessed all over the area of Central Bosnia would start off by what I call "opportunist looting." This is the low-level theft of valuable possessions by some more unruly soldiers who happened to be there. So I'm talking of going into a house and stealing a watch or -- or a painting or something small that would easily be hidden. Then the next stage would be for -- for local civilians to move into the area and start to carry away the sort of things that they could -- they could carry on something like a wheelbarrow or on their own backs or carry between two people. And the final stage was a more concerted effort, which would involve vehicles and tractors arriving at the area and then larger items, such as refrigerators, large pieces of furniture, such as a sofa or whatever, motor cars and things like that would be removed from the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, you also witnessed the situation in which the commander of the 3rd Corps and other commanders invested a lot of effort in order to prevent such things and to arrest those who were involved in looting; however, due to the large scale of the looting, this was not always possible. Are you aware of all these facts?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware directly of any directives issued by either 3 Corps or the HVO headquarters to stop looting; although, just because I did not see it myself does not mean that this did not happen. We were constantly at pains to point out to local commanders at all levels that looting would -- would be seen by the international media as bad for their side and they should wherever possible discourage people from doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Major, just one last question: Orders issued by the army, by the 3rd Corps, brigades, and operations groups were not delivered to the UNPROFOR, so you were not in the position to see the contents of those orders issued by those commanders. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be half correct, then. In my experience there, orders would be delivered to the UNPROFOR headquarters if it would be perceived to show the people issuing the orders in a good light, then. For instance, an order - and I use this as an example - that -- that UNPROFOR vehicles should be given free passage through a particular area would be delivered to the UNPROFOR headquarters. The reality on the ground, however, could be something different. But as far as we were concerned, the commanders at whatever level were doing the right thing and being seen to be obeying the agreement with the United Nations. However, if a military order was of a purely military nature or if the originator of the order did not wish the United Nations to know the contents of that order, then quite clearly they would not be given to anyone in UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, my last question: In the conversation with my co-counsel, you confirmed the fact that you were aware of the fact that the 3rd Corps did take measures in order to prevent the large-scale looting by both civilians and soldiers. Is that correct? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: VAUGHAN KENT-PAYNE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I confirmed that I was aware that an instruction had been issued. But in my opinion, in my experience in the military, there is a big difference between the issuing of an instruction and the physical checking and following up that that order is carried out. And in the British Army, our procedure is that if you issue an order, then it is up to you, the commander, to ensure that that order is carried out. The mere issuing of an order cannot be seen as being -- as being to ensure that the contents of that order is carried out. You have to issue the order and then follow up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major, for the additional explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no additional questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions from the Prosecution, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Major, we would like to thank you for testifying before this Trial Chamber for two days. You have responded very precisely, very completely to the questions put to you by the Prosecution, by the Defence, and by the Judges. I would like to thank you for having given your contribution in revealing the truth. We wish you a happy journey back home, and we wish you a lot of professional success in various international activities, the ones that you mentioned at the beginning of your testimony, when you mentioned all the countries where you served. I'm going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now turning to Mr. Withopf. Can you please advise us about the schedule of witnesses for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, for tomorrow the Prosecution will make available for testimony the witness Cameron Kiggell. He will be available -- he would be available now, but it's our understanding that this court session will be adjourned. The witness will be made available tomorrow. The third witness on our list for this week has arrived and he will also be made available, certainly not prior to Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So tomorrow, Wednesday, we will have at our disposal one witness. Is there anything that the Defence would like to say at this stage? If there's nothing on the part of the Defence and on the part of the Prosecution, I would like to thank you, and I invite you to come back tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of March, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
